analysis.one_liner: Repeals the post-financial-crisis law regulating Wall Street and creating the consumer protection bureau.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the Dodd-Frank financial reform law was introduced with two cosponsors, sent to eight committees, and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would erase the Dodd-Frank Act, the 2010 law passed after the financial crisis that tightened rules on banks, regulated derivatives, and created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Every rule Dodd-Frank changed would snap back to pre-2008 law. The bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks, securities firms, and derivatives traders would benefit most: repeal would remove capital and leverage rules, end the Volcker Rule separating deposit banking from speculative trading, dismantle orderly-liquidation and derivatives rules, and eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, leaving bank oversight largely to pre-crisis regulators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large banks and Wall Street firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Dodd-Frank Act in its entirety and restores the laws it amended as if it had never been enacted.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and taxpayers would bear the cost: mortgage, credit card, and fee protections from the consumer bureau would disappear, riskier bank practices would return without the new capital and derivatives safeguards, and taxpayers would again be more exposed to bailouts if large firms failed, as they were before 2008.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the consumer protections it enforces against credit card, mortgage, and lending abuses, leaving borrowers with the weaker pre-crisis regulatory framework.
Repeal would unwind post-crisis safeguards designed to prevent another taxpayer-funded financial crisis, including rules on bank trading and derivatives that Congress enacted after the 2008 collapse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to a narrow set of large financial firms through lighter regulation; the costs fall broadly on consumers, who would lose dedicated protections, and on taxpayers, who would carry more risk of another systemic crisis. The bill made no attempt to replace the consumer safeguards it repealed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the new Congress, referred to eight committees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michele Bachmann introduced the bill on January 3, 2013, with two Republican cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to eight committees, led by Financial Services, for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
By February 4, 2013, subcommittees in Energy and Commerce and Agriculture held referrals, and the bill took no further action for the rest of the 113th Congress.
The bill expired at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015, without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers: the Dodd-Frank consumer bureau and post-crisis bank rules stayed in place because the bill never advanced. Wall Street firms gained nothing they would have gotten from repeal.

for.name: Michele Bachmann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill repealing Dodd-Frank on the first day of the 113th Congress.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 3, 2013, and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: Seven additional House committees
against.role: Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Budget, Oversight, Ways and Means, Small Business
against.what_they_did: Received referrals and took no action beyond initial subcommittee referrals.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill drew no action in the Republican-run House beyond committee referrals.

industries.note: Repeal would remove Dodd-Frank capital, leverage, and trading rules and eliminate the consumer bureau, freeing the biggest banks from the post-crisis framework. The cost falls on borrowers and on taxpayers who would again face bailout exposure.
Dodd-Frank brought swap trading under regulation and clearing requirements; repeal would restore the pre-2008 unregulated market. Traders would regain flexibility at the public's risk.

Repeal would end consumer-bureau oversight of mortgages, credit cards, and lending. Lenders could reinstate practices the post-crisis rules restricted, with borrowers paying through fees and risky products.
